newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Cyprus Minerals fears Zaire impact in Zambia.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus Minerals fears Zaire impact in Zambia.

text.p: Cyprus Amax Minerals Co said on Thursday that it was apprehensive about the impact the Zairean conflict could have on operations at its recently acquired Kansanshi copper mine in Zambia's North-Western Province.
"While Zambia is peaceful, it is unclear what impact there will be from the current events in Zaire," Cyprus Amax director for business development, Todd Anderson, told an investment conference.
"The Kansanshi mine lies just minutes from the Zairean border and the region has been the site of significant refugee activity in the past during events on the Zairean side of the border."
Cyprus Amax signed an agreement for the acquisation of 80 percent of Kansanshi mine in January.
Kansanshi was the first ZCCM mine to be sold under Zambia's ambitious privatisation of state assets.
Anderson said Cyprus Amax was also concerned about the high incidence of HIV infection in the country.
"There will certainly be a diminishing pool of trained Zambians, both at a labour level and at a management level by the time we would expect to begin operations in the early 2,000s," Anderson said.

"This will occur during a period when there is likely to be a higher demand for labour in Zambia, not only from new and existing copper projects, but also from businesses which will be formed as assets are privatised to support those privatised or developing operations," he added.
Other problems that faced Cyprus Amax operations in Zambia were inadequate and poor infrastructure and logistics.
Anderson said the company was worried by the lack of a railway linking Solwezi, where Kansanshi mine is based, to the Copperbelt, and the poor state of roads in the area.

The distance from the mine to the most feasible port, Dar-es-Salaam, at 2,000 km, was too long, while the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA), linking Zambia's Copperbelt to port Dar-es-Salaam, was inefficient.

"There may be alternatives such as re-establishing the line to the port of Benguela, which would be shorter...than going to Dar-es-Salaam, assuming permanence of Angolan stability as laid out in the peace accord," Anderson said.
Despite the problems, Anderson said Cyprus Amax was upbeat about the Kansanshi project and would vie for other concessions elsewhere in the country.
"In our opinion, the opportunities we see outweigh the challenges. We believe most of the challenges...can and will be resolved over time," he said.
Cyprux Amax estimates Kansanshi to have a reserve grade of around 1.5 percent copper with a material amount of gold as a by-product.

"This reserve grade is equivalent to four or five times the reserve grade found in our domestic (American) deposits, which we are mining at a substsantial profit even at those lower grades," Anderson said.

"The Kansanshi deposit gives us the opportunity to apply the same technologies and cost saving operational methods to a deposit where savings will equate to a high dollars per dollar spent," he added.
